title: The Maids adapted by Kip Williams at St Ann’s Warehouse #themaids #st...
transcript: I really enjoyed this in the moment but I'm struggling to articulate any lasting impression in hindsight. The Maids is a satirical psychological thriller about Claire and Solange, a pair of sisters who have been working for Madame for years but fantasize about killing her when she's gone. Upon learning that one of their diabolical plans to sabotage Madame is crumbling, they agree to finish her off when she gets home. I’m not familiar with the original 1947 version of this play, but this production is very modern, with references to Bad Bunny, red carpets, and social media. There are also screens, which aren't used as heavily as they are in some other pieces by Kip Williams, such as Sarah Snook’s solo Dorian Gray, but they still add a modern and comedic layer to the story. The outstanding performances and tense underscoring also elevate the experience, but you can't help but wonder if the production is overwhelming you with stimuli to distract from an otherwise middling plot with one dimensional characters. Madame is unnamed and over the top to the point of caricature, yet she's arguably the one we learn the most about. The sisters, while capturing the central themes of class-related resentment, jealousy, and repressed desire, are not very developed. Regardless, the actors bring to their roles a good amount of emotional clarity that keeps the show captivating the entire time. Things get intentionally muddy toward the end, with reality and performance blurring for both the audience and the characters on stage. While I was curious enough to look up some interpretations of the ending afterwards, I wasn't invested enough to expend much energy interpreting it myself. Although I enjoyed it in the moment, I can tell it won't stick with me because it was ultimately more interesting than it was affecting. With that, another program for my collection.
